Marx.description: Refers to Karl Marx, the philosopher and revolutionary, whose statue is present in the children's garden and whose life is taught as an example of service to humanity.

Darwin.description: Refers to Charles Darwin, the scientist known for the theory of evolution, whose story is included in the curriculum.

kurta.description: A traditional Indian long shirt worn by both boys and girls.

untouchables.description: A term historically used in India to refer to people considered outside the caste system and subjected to severe social discrimination.

Esperanto.description: An international auxiliary language created in the late 19th century, used here as the basis for the 'universal language' of the future.

Latin.description: The classical language of ancient Rome, another root source for the universal language.

Teutonic.description: A historical term for the Germanic languages of Europe.

Roman.description: Likely refers to the Romance languages derived from Latin.

Slav.description: Refers to the Slavic languages of Eastern Europe.

Celtic.description: A family of languages spoken in parts of Western Europe, such as Ireland and Wales.

China.description: A country in East Asia, mentioned as a place where the universal language is spoken.

Japan.description: An East Asian country, also adopting the universal language.

Siam.description: The former name of Thailand, included among countries where the universal language is used.

Persian.description: A language spoken from Peshawar to Baghdad, described as related to Bharati.

Peshawar.description: A city in present-day Pakistan, marking the western extent of Persian's range.

Baghdad.description: The capital of Iraq, marking the western boundary of the Persian-speaking region.

Africa.description: A continent mentioned as a place where European languages are spoken.

bioscopes.description: Early motion picture devices or projectors, used here for educational purposes.

Universal Hostel.description: A special residential facility where children live and speak only the universal language.

quinine.description: A bitter medicinal compound used to treat malaria, referenced metaphorically for unpleasantness.

M.A.s.description: Abbreviation for 'Master of Arts', a postgraduate academic degree.

Acharya Vasistha.description: A distinguished scholar and teacher at the School of Philosophy, renowned for his expertise in Indian and global philosophical thought.

Upadhyaya Vishwa.description: A figure mentioned at the end of the chapter, likely a teacher or administrator involved in the governance system at Nalanda.

Language-Archaeology.description: A specialized school at Nalanda University focusing on the study of languages and archaeology, including primary historical sources.

Baibhara Giri.description: A hill in Rajgriha, transformed in the future to house a major astronomical observatory.

Iran.description: A country in the Middle East, included among the ancient civilizations studied at Nalanda.

Sumatra.description: An island in Indonesia, included among the regions explored for ancient Indian civilization.

Central Asia.description: A region north of India, referenced as a site of historical research.

Suryanarayan.description: A village near Nalanda, mentioned as no longer existing in the future setting.

Nalanda Press.description: The printing press at Nalanda University, responsible for publishing books and scientific journals.

Bhairavji.description: A name by which the Buddha statue was known among rural people in the twentieth century.

stupa.description: A dome-shaped Buddhist monument, often containing relics and used as a place of meditation.

canopy.description: A decorative covering, often placed over statues or sacred objects.

hostels.description: In this context, residential facilities for students, each functioning like a small village.

Brahmin-Rajput-Sheikh-Sayyid.description: These are traditional Indian and Islamic caste and community groups historically associated with social hierarchy and privilege.

Shimla.description: A city in northern India, historically known as the summer capital during British rule, referenced here as a former privilege for government officials.

Narang River.description: A river in Brazil, South America, on whose banks the Universal City is located in the novel.

Brazil.description: A country in South America, chosen as the site for the Universal City and the Universal Assembly in the novel.

South America.description: A continent referenced as the location of the Universal City and the seat of the Universal Assembly.

Universal City.description: A futuristic city on the equator in Brazil, serving as the headquarters of the Universal Assembly and government.

Universal Assembly.description: The highest global governing body in the novel, composed of representatives from around the world.

Universal Era.description: A new calendar era inaugurated with the founding of the Universal Government, marking a new epoch in world history.

panch.description: An elected representative in the village assembly, with one panch chosen for every hundred people.

tehsil.description: A sub-district administrative division in India, historically grouping several villages together.

crore.description: A unit in the Indian numbering system equal to ten million (10,000,000).

Yusuf.description: The president of the Magadh Administrative Assembly and a comrade of the narrator, Yusuf welcomes the travelers at Patna station.

Malda.description: A famous variety of mango from the region around Malda, a city in West Bengal, India.

Langda.description: A well-known variety of mango, originally from northern India, especially Uttar Pradesh and Bihar.

Sumeru.description: A term from Hindu and Buddhist cosmology referring to the mythic Mount Meru, here used to denote the North Pole.

Kumeru.description: In Hindu cosmology, the antipodal counterpart to Sumeru, here representing the South Pole.

Darjeeling.description: A town in West Bengal, India, known for its tea and as a Himalayan gateway.

Sadiya.description: A town in Assam, India, serving as a route across the Himalayas.

Himalayas.description: The mountain range separating the plains of the Indian subcontinent from the Tibetan Plateau.

Altai Mountains.description: A mountain range in Central and East Asia, crossed by the railway.

Yunnan.description: A province in southwest China, part of the railway network.

Chittagong.description: A port city in Bangladesh, linked by railway.

Assam.description: A state in northeastern India, part of the railway network.

Malaya.description: A historical region on the Malay Peninsula, now part of Malaysia.

Singapore.description: A major city-state in Southeast Asia, connected by tunnel to Sumatra.

Yarkand.description: A city in Xinjiang, China, on the railway route.

Kashgar.description: A city in Xinjiang, China, on the railway route.

Turkestan.description: A historical region in Central Asia, traversed by the railway.

Tashkent.description: The capital of Uzbekistan, on the railway route.

Samarkand.description: A historic city in Uzbekistan, on the railway route.

Afghanistan.description: A country in South-Central Asia, connected by railway.

Turkey.description: A country at the crossroads of Europe and Asia, on the railway route.

Arabia.description: The Arabian Peninsula, included in the railway network.

Russia.description: The largest country in the world, entered by the railway via the Ural Mountains.

Ural Mountains.description: A mountain range in Russia, marking the boundary between Europe and Asia.

Constantinople.description: The historical name for Istanbul, Turkey, where tunnels connect Asia and Europe.

France.description: A country in Western Europe, connected to England by tunnel.

England.description: A country in the United Kingdom, connected to France by tunnel.

Suez Canal.description: A man-made waterway in Egypt, now with a tunnel-railway linking Asia and Africa.

Sahara.description: The vast desert in North Africa, transformed into a sea in the novel.

Bering Strait.description: The strait connecting Asia and North America, now with a railway tunnel.

Alaska.description: A U.S. state in northwest North America, reached by train from Siberia.

Canada.description: A country in North America, traversed by the railway.

United States.description: A country in North America, traversed by the railway.

Panama Canal.description: A waterway in Central America, now crossed by a railway tunnel.

Colombia.description: A country in South America, on the railway route.

Peru.description: A country in South America, on the railway route.

Bolivia.description: A country in South America, on the railway route.

Chile.description: A country in South America, on the railway route.

Argentina.description: A country in South America, on the railway route.

Uruguay.description: A country in South America, on the railway route.

Patagonia.description: A region in southern South America, included in the railway network.

Scott.description: A reference to Robert Falcon Scott, the British Antarctic explorer.

Magadh.description: A historic region in Bihar, India, now a republic and major fruit producer.

Banaras.description: Also known as Varanasi or Kashi, a historic city in Uttar Pradesh, India.

Kashi Karwat.description: A historic locality or feature of old Banaras, now vanished.

Kachauri Gali.description: A famous lane in Banaras, known for its kachauris (savory snacks).

Manikarnika.description: A famous ghat (riverfront) in Banaras, known for cremations.

Dashashwamedh.description: A prominent ghat in Banaras, known for religious ceremonies.

Satti of Dashashwamedh.description: A reference to a site or practice at Dashashwamedh Ghat, possibly related to sati (widow immolation).

Visheshwarganj.description: A market area in Banaras, historically known for granaries.

Dalmandi.description: A locality in Banaras, formerly known for its brothels.

Rishipatan Mrigadava.description: The ancient name for Sarnath, near Banaras, where the Buddha gave his first sermon.

Sarnath.description: A historical site near Banaras, associated with Buddhism.

Ashoka Bhavan.description: A grand building in Patna, modeled after Vasubandhu Bhavan of Nalanda.

Vasubandhu Bhavan.description: A notable building in Nalanda, serving as an architectural model for Ashoka Bhavan.

ghats.description: Stepped embankments or riverfronts, especially along the Ganges in Banaras, used for bathing and religious rituals.

kachauris.description: A type of savory fried pastry popular in northern India, especially in Banaras.

guru-guru.description: A chant or repetitive phrase associated with religious rituals or priests at the ghats.

Satti.description: Likely a variant spelling of 'sati', the historical practice of widow immolation, here referencing a site or custom at Dashashwamedh Ghat.

stupas.description: Dome-shaped Buddhist structures that serve as places of meditation and house relics.

Assi.description: A locality in Varanasi, situated near the Kashi Vishwavidyalaya.

Kashi Vishwavidyalaya.description: Also known as Benares Hindu University, a prestigious university in Varanasi, India.

Indraprastha.description: An ancient city, now described as an independent republic in the novel's future India.

Vatsa.description: A region or republic, historically a Mahajanapada (ancient kingdom) in northern India.

Panchala.description: An ancient kingdom, here depicted as a modern independent republic.

Surasena.description: A historical region, now a republic, that has absorbed many former principalities.

Punjab.description: A northern region of India, here described as having many democracies.

Lahore.description: A major city, serving as the capital of a democracy in Punjab or Kashmir.

Takshashila University.description: An ancient center of learning, now restored to its former glory, famous for Ayurveda.

Rajasthan.description: A region in western India, historically home to Rajput principalities.

Rajput.description: A group of warrior clans from Rajasthan, whose former principalities are now unified.

Sindh.description: A region in present-day Pakistan, known for its agricultural abundance and the great canal.

Bikaner.description: A city in Rajasthan, historically arid but now fertile due to the Sindh canal.

Ajmer.description: A city in Rajasthan, serving as its capital in the novel's future.

Karachi.description: A major port city, now the capital of Sindh.

Saurashtra.description: A region in western India, visited by the narrator.

Gujarat.description: A state in western India, known for cotton cultivation.

Malwa.description: A region in central India, also noted for cotton production.

Vidarbha.description: A region in eastern Maharashtra, part of the cotton belt.

Maharashtra.description: A large state in western India, divided into North and South republics in the novel.

Hyderabad.description: A former princely state, now divided into four republics.

Dravid.description: Refers to the Dravidian region or people of southern India.

Utkal.description: An ancient name for the region of Odisha in eastern India.

Himalayan states.description: The states located in the Himalayan mountain region, part of the unified India.

pandits.description: Learned scholars or teachers, especially of Sanskrit and Hindu law or philosophy.

Darbhanga.description: A district in the Indian state of Bihar, historically known for agriculture and cultural significance.

charas.description: A form of hand-made cannabis resin originating from the Indian subcontinent.

toddy.description: An alcoholic beverage made from the sap of various species of palm trees, commonly consumed in South Asia.

kahwa.description: A traditional green tea preparation flavored with spices, popular in Kashmir and parts of Central Asia.

sawan.description: A type of small-grained millet (barnyard millet) cultivated in India, often considered an inferior grain.

kodon.description: A variety of millet (kodo millet) grown in India, known for its hardiness and use as a staple food among poorer communities.

mandua.description: Also known as ragi or finger millet, a nutritious grain widely grown in India, especially in hilly regions.
